text.p: President Fidel Ramos leapt in the air, others waved yellow ribbons and a top churchman warned against authoritarianism as the Philippines on Tuesday marked the anniversary of the 1986 revolt that ousted Ferdinand Marcos.

Seeking to revive the national unity that sparked the "people power" upheaval against Marcos, Ramos and a crowd estimated by police at 10,000 revisited Manila's Edsa highway where the four-day uprising that gripped the world began.
But a bitter row over a campaign by Ramos supporters to revise the constitution to allow him to stay in power when his term ends next year, clouded the celebration.
Ramos sought to defuse the controversy by pledging anew in a speech that he would step down when his six-year tenure ends in June 1998.
He said one of his remaining goals was to reduce poverty from around 40 percent "to 30 percent by 1998 -- the year when I relinquish my watch on the presidency".

Ramos, clad in blue jeans similar to those he wore during the 1986 revolt, leapt in the air five times, re-enacting his jumps at Edsa 11 years ago when news swept the city that Marcos had fled the country to Hawaii, where he later died in exile.
Cardinal Jaime Sin, the Philippines' most influential prelate who helped ignite the anti-Marcos revolt, praised Ramos for his renewed pledge to step down.
"Happily, the president...has refused to sully the limited legitimacy of his incumbency with the unlimited shamelessness of a megalomaniac despot," Sin said at a Mass highlighting the celebration.
But the Manila archbishop, clearly referring to presidential advisers, attacked "the dubious forces" he said were trying to convince Ramos to change his mind.
Groups favouring the charter changes say letting Ramos run again will ensure continuity of his economic reform agenda that has given the country one of Asia's most vibrant economies.

It was Sin's radio broadcast in 1986 that brought up to a million civilians onto the 14-lane Edsa highway to protect Ramos, then defence secretary Juan Ponce Enrile and about 300 army mutineers against Marcos' advancing tanks.
Ramos, who underwent a vascular operation in December, showed he had fully recovered as he marched in the afternoon sun down the highway to shake hands with and hug supporters.
He also danced with some of the 600 "Edsa babies" -- children born during the revolt -- who attended the event.
Former president Corazon Aquino, who inspired the uprising against Marcos, joined Ramos and Sin in the celebration.
Aquino said on Monday she was convinced Ramos was sincere in his promise to step down, but urged him to dispel all doubts by arranging for "a peaceful transfer of power" to his successor.
Many in the crowd waved yellow ribbons or wore yellow shirts, Aquino's theme colour in her campaign to oust Marcos.
The Philippine Daily Inquirer said the 1986 revolt had fallen short of its promise, noting Marcos's wife, Imelda, and their associates were back in power as members of congress.

"Up to now there has been no restitution, no retribution, no punishment," the newspaper said in an editorial. "The billions stolen from public coffers have not been returned. Justice still has to be done to the people, and specially to the victims of human rights violations of the Marcos dictatorship."
Marcos was in power for 20 years before being forced to flee the country.
